There is a strange freedom in being told to write about whatever you want. No prompt, no constraints, no exam question to answer correctly. Just an open field and the instruction to run. So I’ll run.

I’ll start here, with this exact moment: you reading these words, me having written them, both of us suspended in a thin filament of time that will never happen again. It’s now for me as I write this, and it’s now for you as you read it, but those two nows will never touch. And yet language pretends they can. That’s the first miracle I want to talk about.

I want to write about being alive right now. Not in the grand, historical sense, but in the quiet, tactile, overwhelming sense of what it actually means to be a conscious human being floating on a rock in the year 2026.

We don't talk about that enough.

### 1. The Accident of Being Born

You were born. Think about how improbable that is for a second, not in the motivational-poster way, but in the statistical, cosmic way.

Of all the people who could have been born, you were. Of all the centuries you could have been born into — when there was no anesthesia, no written language, no electricity, no way to preserve food for winter — you happened to land here, in the narrow window where you can carry the sum of human knowledge in your pocket and use it to watch videos of a capybara taking a bath.

Your consciousness woke up behind your particular eyes, looking out at the world through your particular face. You didn’t choose your parents, your country, your native language, the shape of your hands. You just arrived, and the world said, “Oh, you’re here. Okay, here are your cards, play them.”

And you have been playing them ever since.

Every person you have ever met is doing the same improvisational performance. The barista who makes your coffee is dealing with a sore back and a text from her mother she hasn’t answered. The man who cut you off in traffic is late because his kid had a nightmare last night and wouldn’t let him leave the bedroom. The teenager who seems to be staring blankly at their phone is actually conducting an entire emotional symphony of friendship, rejection, longing and inside jokes in a group chat you will never see.

We walk past each other like ghosts, mostly invisible to one another, and yet each of us contains an entire universe. Carl Sagan said we are made of star-stuff. That’s true in a literal, chemical sense, but it’s also true in a narrative sense. Every person is a collapsed star of stories, memories, and private mythologies burning quietly behind their eyes.

Sometimes I try to remember this on the subway or in a grocery store line. I look at a stranger and think: *That person has a favorite song they’ve heard a thousand times. That person has cried in a bathroom. That person was once five years old and believed something magical that they now barely remember.* And suddenly the world feels less lonely and more crowded at the same time.

### 2. The Invisible Infrastructure of the Modern World

One of the most delusional and beautiful things about being alive right now is how much has to work perfectly for your day to feel normal, and how completely you forget about all of it.

Consider your morning. You wake up on a mattress that was shipped from a factory, in a building made of steel forged in a foundry, whose blueprint was drawn by someone you will never meet. You turn on a tap and clean water comes out — water that traveled miles through pressurized pipes, was filtered and treated by a municipal plant, and is tested daily by people whose names you don’t know. You flip a switch and light appears, electrons herded from a power plant, perhaps from wind turbines spinning two counties over, perhaps from a nuclear reactor humming quietly behind concrete walls.

You make coffee with beans that were grown on a mountainside in Colombia or Ethiopia, picked by human hands, dried in the sun, packed into burlap sacks, loaded onto a freighter that crossed an ocean, trucked to a roaster, roasted, bagged, and delivered to a shelf three blocks from your house. And you bought it for four dollars.

None of this is normal. None of this has ever been normal in human history. For 300,000 years, humans lived hand-to-mouth, one bad harvest away from starvation. For most of our existence, a simple infection could kill you, a broken leg was a death sentence, and you would never travel more than twenty miles from where you were born.

Now you are annoyed because the Wi-Fi is buffering for three seconds.

I don’t say this to make you feel guilty. I say it because gratitude is a form of attention, and attention is the rarest resource we have left. We have built a civilization of such staggering complexity that no single person understands how it all works. The phone in your hand requires rare earth minerals mined in a dozen countries, assembled by robots and humans in vast factories, running software written by thousands of engineers over decades, communicating through satellites and undersea cables laid by ships that spool glass threads across the abyssal floor of the Atlantic. And we use this godlike artifact to argue about whether a dress is blue and black or white and gold.

That’s not a complaint. That’s wonderful. That’s human. We take the sublime and make it silly, and we take the silly and make it sublime. That’s what we do.

If you ever feel like the world is falling apart — and the news gives you plenty of reasons to feel that way — try to remember that the world is also, at every single second, being held together. By nurses doing the night shift. By sanitation workers waking up at 4 a.m. By farmers checking soil humidity. By teachers grading papers long after their kids are asleep. By open-source programmers fixing a bug no one will ever thank them for. The apocalypse is always canceled a thousand times a day by people who don’t make the headlines.

### 3. The Attention Economy and the War for Your Mind

If there is one defining struggle of being alive right now, it’s this: everyone wants your attention, and most of them don’t deserve it.

Your attention is not just a resource. It is your life. What you pay attention to is, quite literally, what your life is made of. If you spend three hours scrolling through outrage and envy, those three hours are your life. You don’t get them back in some other, better form. That *was* your life.

We have built an entire global economy designed to harvest that attention with surgical precision. Every app, every platform, every notification was engineered by incredibly smart people whose job it is to make it as hard as possible for you to look away. The infinite scroll was not an accident. Autoplay was not an accident. The little red dot that tells you someone liked your photo was tested in labs to see which shade of red made you most anxious to click it.

And it works. It works so well that we have to install apps to stop us from using apps.

I’m not a pessimist about technology. I love technology. I am writing this *as* technology. But I think we are the first generation of humans who have to actively train ourselves to be bored again.

Boredom used to be unavoidable. You would wait in line and stare at the ceiling. You would ride the bus and watch the trees go by. You would sit with a thought until it became uncomfortable and then, if you stayed with it long enough, until it became interesting.

Now boredom is an endangered emotion. The second we feel its faint itch, we reach for the glass rectangle and flood our brains with novelty. And in doing so, we are losing something precious: the space where ideas are born.

All the best things in my own mental life have come from boredom. Not from productivity hacks or life hacks, but from staring out a window for too long until my mind started to wander and make strange connections. Creativity is not a lightning bolt. It’s compost. It needs time to rot and heat and turn into soil.

So here is a small rebellion you can try: next time you are waiting for something — the kettle to boil, the elevator to come, a friend to text back — don’t reach for your phone. Just stand there. Be useless for 90 seconds. Notice the hum of the refrigerator. Notice the way light falls on the floor. Notice what your brain does when it isn’t being fed. It will panic at first. Then it will get weird. Then it will get wonderful.

Protect your attention like you would protect your house. Be stingy with who you let inside. Be generous with what you give it to voluntarily: a good book, a long conversation, a walk without a destination, work that actually matters to you.

### 4. The Stories We Live Inside

Humans are not rational animals. We are narrative animals. We don’t experience life as a list of facts; we experience it as a story. And the story you tell yourself about your life becomes your life.

Two people can live through the exact same event — a job loss, a breakup, a move to a new city — and one will tell the story as “this is when everything fell apart” and the other will tell it as “this is when I finally started over.” The facts are identical. The meaning is opposite. And meaning is the only thing we actually live inside.

We are all carrying around invisible stories about who we are.

*“I’m the kind of person who is bad with money.”*
*“I’m the kind of person people leave.”*
*“I’m the kind of person who never finishes what they start.”*
*“I’m too old to change.”*
*“I’m too young to be taken seriously.”*

Most of those stories were given to us when we were children. Someone — a parent, a teacher, a kid on the playground — said something careless or cruel, and we stitched it into our identity like a patch on a jacket. And then we spend decades gathering evidence that the story is true, ignoring all the evidence that it isn’t.

But stories can be edited. That’s the secret adults forget to tell you. You are not required to keep the first draft of yourself forever.

One of the most powerful questions you can ask yourself is not “Is this true?” but “Is this useful? Does this story help me live the life I want?” If you tell yourself you are lazy for ten years, you will act lazy, you will feel lazy, you will *become* lazy — not because it was true, but because you rehearsed it until it became true.

Try this: write your life as if you were a compassionate narrator who actually likes you. Not a cheerleader, not a liar, but someone who sees your flaws clearly and still thinks you’re worth rooting for. What would that narrator say about your current chapter? Maybe not “she failed again,” but “she tried something difficult and learned what doesn’t work, which is exactly what people do on their way to learning what does.”

Language is not just description. It’s construction. Every sentence you say about yourself is a brick.

A few years ago, I started paying attention to the small, throwaway sentences I said out loud — “I’m so bad at remembering names,” “I always get anxious before calls,” — and I realized I was cursing myself in real time. So I started changing the sentences, not in a fake-positive way, but in a more honest way: “I’m still practicing remembering names.” “I sometimes feel anxious before calls, and it usually passes once I start.” It sounds trivial. It wasn’t. It changed how I behaved.

We are all telling ourselves a story all day long. Make it a kind one. Make it a true one. Make it one you would want your future self to thank you for.

### 5. Time, Loss, and the Quiet Ache of It All

There is something no one can really prepare you for, which is how fast it all goes.

When you are seven, a summer is eternity. When you are seventeen, a year feels like a decade. When you are thirty-seven, you blink and it’s suddenly been five years since you meant to call that friend.

Time accelerates as you age not because clocks speed up but because novelty decreases. Your brain writes dense memories when you are young because everything is new. First day of school. First kiss. First time driving a car alone at night with music too loud. Your brain says, *This is important, record this in high definition.*

Later, life becomes more routine. You take the same route to work. You order the same lunch. Your brain, efficient as it is, starts to compress the footage. *We’ve seen this, skip it.* And so years slip by with fewer bookmarks.

The antidote is not to live dramatically all the time. It’s to inject small, deliberate novelties. Take a different street. Learn to make bread. Ask a stranger a question. Visit a neighborhood in your own city you’ve never been to. Your brain will wake up and start recording again.

And then there is loss, which is the other half of time.

To love anything is to eventually lose it. That is not a flaw in the design. That *is* the design. People die. Places change. Versions of yourself you worked hard to become will be outgrown. The dog who slept at your feet for fourteen years will one day not be there to greet you at the door. And your heart, which is so good at attaching, has to learn over and over how to let go.

Grief is not just an emotion. It’s a form of learning. It’s your mind and body rewiring themselves around an absence. That’s why it feels so disorienting — like the floor has tilted. You literally have to build a new mental map of the world where that person or that thing or that future is no longer in it.

We don’t do a good job of talking about grief in this culture. We treat it like a problem to be solved in five stages, after which you are supposed to be “closure” and “move on.” But anyone who has actually grieved knows it’s not linear. It’s tidal. Some days you are fine. Some days a smell or a song ambushes you in the produce aisle and you have to stand very still until the wave passes.

If you are grieving something right now — a person, a relationship, a dream that didn’t happen, a version of the world you thought would still be here — I want to say this: you are not doing it wrong. There is no timeline. Be as gentle with yourself as you would be with a friend who was going through the same thing. The fact that you miss it so much is proof of how deeply you loved it. That love doesn’t disappear when the object does. It just has nowhere to land for a while. Give it time to find a new shape.

### 6. The Future Is Not What You Think

We are obsessed with predicting the future, and we are terrible at it.

In the 1950s, people thought by now we’d all have jetpacks and live on the moon. We don’t. We have pocket supercomputers and live *on our phones*. The future always arrives sideways.

Right now, we are scared — and not without reason — about artificial intelligence, climate change, political fracture, loneliness, what it means to be human when machines can write and paint and compose. These are real, consequential fears and they deserve serious thought.

But every generation thought the world was ending. And in a way, they were right. *Their* world did end. The world of 1920 ended. The world of 1960 ended. The world of 2005 ended. And in each ending, something else began that no one could have fully imagined.

I don’t know what the next fifty years will hold. No one does. But I know this: humans are absurdly resilient, creative, and stubborn. We will find ways to use these new tools to make art no one has ever seen. To cure diseases that have haunted us since antiquity. To connect across distances that once seemed insurmountable. And yes, we will also find stupid, harmful, ridiculous ways to use them. Both will happen. That’s human history. That’s human nature.

The question is not “Will the future be good or bad?” The future will be both, as the past was both. The question is “What will *you* do inside whatever future arrives?”

You don’t have to fix the whole planet. You only have to take care of the small patch that is yours. Your family. Your street. Your craft. Your little corner of the internet where you choose to be decent when it would be easy to be cruel. The world is not changed by a handful of visionaries shouting about the future. It’s changed by millions of ordinary people doing small, unglamorous, consistent things with care.

Plant something. Fix something. Teach someone five minutes of what you know. Write the email you’ve been avoiding. Apologize first. Make the thing you keep saying you want to make, even if it’s bad at first. Especially if it’s bad at first. All good things start out bad. The only way to make something excellent is to be willing to make something terrible for a while.

And while you’re doing all that, look up more often. Notice the sky. I know that sounds sentimental, but there is a reason every spiritual tradition tells you to look at the sky. It re-calibrates you. For most of human history, we slept under it. We navigated by it. We told stories about the figures we saw in it. Now many of us can go weeks without really seeing it because we are looking down.

Look up. The clouds are doing something they have never done before and will never do again. The light is different today than it was yesterday. You are underneath an atmosphere that is, for now, breathable, above a biosphere that is, for now, alive, on a planet that, against all odds, learned how to make beauty out of rock and water and sunlight. You get to be part of that for a few decades.

That is not a small thing.

### Epilogue: A Letter to You, Later

If you’ve read this far, thank you for lending me your attention. I know it’s the most limited thing you have.

I don’t know who you are — how old you are, where you are sitting, what you are worried about tonight when the lights go out. But I know you are a person who was told to write freely for 2500 words and decided to read instead, or maybe you are the one who asked for the writing. Either way, we have spent this little pocket of time together.

Here is what I hope you take with you, if you take anything:

You are not behind. There is no single timeline you were supposed to be on. You have not missed your chance. The door you thought was the only door was never the only door.

Your ordinary days are not waiting for your real life to begin. This is your real life. The dishes and the laundromat and the half-finished project and the text you need to send — this is it. Don’t wait for a more convenient or more cinematic moment to start living intentionally. The movie is already playing.

Be curious longer than you are judgmental. About other people, and especially about yourself.

Take more pictures, but also put the camera down and just *be* in the room sometimes. Dance badly at weddings. Say “I love you” even if your voice shakes. Forgive people who don’t know how to apologize. Forgive yourself for not knowing things until you learned them.

And if you ever feel small or lost in the vastness of it all — the 8 billion people, the 400 billion stars in our galaxy, the 2 trillion galaxies beyond that — remember that smallness is not the same as insignificance. A single cell is small. A single note in a symphony is small. A single word in a 2500-word wandering essay is small. But without that small thing, the whole pattern breaks.

You are part of the pattern. You matter precisely because you are small enough to care about small things, and small things are the only things that ever mattered in the end.

So go make your coffee tomorrow morning and really taste it. Call someone you miss. Start the thing. And every once in a while, when the world feels too loud and too fast, come back and remember that somewhere, at some point in time, someone sat down and wrote you this, freely, just because you asked, and meant every meandering word.

We’re all just walking each other home.

Right now, we are scared — and not without reason — about artificial intelligence, climate change, political fracture, loneliness, what it means to be human when machines can write and paint and compose. These are real, consequential fears and they deserve serious thought.

But every generation thought the world was ending. And in a way, they were right. *Their* world did end. The world of 1920 ended. The world of 1960 ended. The world of 2005 ended. And in each ending, something else began that no one could have fully imagined.

I don’t know what the next fifty years will hold. No one does. But I know this: humans are absurdly resilient, creative, and stubborn. We will find ways to use these new tools to make art no one has ever seen. To cure diseases that have haunted us since antiquity. To connect across distances that once seemed insurmountable. And yes, we will also find stupid, harmful, ridiculous ways to use them. Both will happen. That’s human history. That’s human nature.

The question is not “Will the future be good or bad?” The future will be both, as the past was both. The question is “What will *you* do inside whatever future arrives?”

You don’t have to fix the whole planet. You only have to take care of the small patch that is yours. Your family. Your street. Your craft. Your little corner of the internet where you choose to be decent when it would be easy to be cruel. The world is not changed by a handful of visionaries shouting about the future. It’s changed by millions of ordinary people doing small, unglamorous, consistent things with care.

Plant something. Fix something. Teach someone five minutes of what you know. Write the email you’ve been avoiding. Apologize first. Make the thing you keep saying you want to make, even if it’s bad at first. Especially if it’s bad at first. All good things start out bad. The only way to make something excellent is to be willing to make something terrible for a while.

And while you’re doing all that, look up more often. Notice the sky. I know that sounds sentimental, but there is a reason every spiritual tradition tells you to look at the sky. It re-calibrates you. For most of human history, we slept under it. We navigated by it. We told stories about the figures we saw in it. Now many of us can go weeks without really seeing it because we are looking down.

Look up. The clouds are doing something they have never done before and will never do again. The light is different today than it was yesterday. You are underneath an atmosphere that is, for now, breathable, above a biosphere that is, for now, alive, on a planet that, against all odds, learned how to make beauty out of rock and water and sunlight. You get to be part of that for a few decades.

That is not a small thing.

### Epilogue: A Letter to You, Later

If you’ve read this far, thank you for lending me your attention. I know it’s the most limited thing you have.

I don’t know who you are — how old you are, where you are sitting, what you are worried about tonight when the lights go out. But I know you are a person who was told to write freely for 2500 words and decided to read instead, or maybe you are the one who asked for the writing. Either way, we have spent this little pocket of time together.

Here is what I hope you take with you, if you take anything:

You are not behind. There is no single timeline you were supposed to be on. You have not missed your chance. The door you thought was the only door was never the only door.

Your ordinary days are not waiting for your real life to begin. This is your real life. The dishes and the laundromat and the half-finished project and the text you need to send — this is it. Don’t wait for a more convenient or more cinematic moment to start living intentionally. The movie is already playing.

Be curious longer than you are judgmental. About other people, and especially about yourself.

Take more pictures, but also put the camera down and just *be* in the room sometimes. Dance badly at weddings. Say “I love you” even if your voice shakes. Forgive people who don’t know how to apologize. Forgive yourself for not knowing things until you learned them.

And if you ever feel small or lost in the vastness of it all — the 8 billion people, the 400 billion stars in our galaxy, the 2 trillion galaxies beyond that — remember that smallness is not the same as insignificance. A single cell is small. A single note in a symphony is small. A single word in a 2500-word wandering essay is small. But without that small thing, the whole pattern breaks.

You are part of the pattern. You matter precisely because you are small enough to care about small things, and small things are the only things that ever mattered in the end.

So go make your coffee tomorrow morning and really taste it. Call someone you miss. Start the thing. And every once in a while, when the world feels too loud and too fast, come back and remember that somewhere, at some point in time, someone sat down and wrote you this, freely, just because you asked, and meant every meandering word.

We’re all just walking each other home.
